articles.title: A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone
articles.full_text:
For years, the definition of a premium smartphone depended on its cameras, processors, and how light it felt when you stowed it in your pocket. The iPhone Duo challenges that concept by asking consumers to pay more for a fundamentally different smartphone experience, even if it means sacrificing what they’ve long thought of as high-end features.

In a little under a month of using the Duo, I’ve found that the trade-offs I was initially concerned about matter far less to me than I had expected. What’s been more interesting is how the Duo’s foldable form factor has changed my everyday habits, including how I interact with apps, which apps I use, and how I organize and personalize the phone itself.

I also easily forgot a number of my initial concerns about switching to the Duo. The apps, for the most part, are now optimized for the Duo; I’ve reacquainted myself with Touch ID; and I don’t miss the Pro Max camera on most days.

That’s not to say the Duo doesn’t have its shortcomings. I still miss that telephoto lens sometimes, and I’m still longing for Face ID — though not as much sinceApple shipped a face unlock featurein the latest update. But after a month of using the Duo, I’ve found these compromises have had less of an impact on my day-to-day experience compared with the benefits that the new form factor brings.

I was surprised by how much I’ve grown to appreciate the Duo’s multitasking capabilities. Initially, I didn’t think I’d regularly use it to view two apps side by side, given the still fairly limited screen space even while the phone is unfolded, especially compared with an iPad. But I’ve found myself snapping apps to both halves of the screen more often than I had imagined.

For starters, Apple has made this side-by-side mode incredibly intuitive and easy to use — you simply drag the app over to the left or right side of the screen and drop it into the target box that appears.

I have regularly taken advantage of this feature to do all sorts of things.

I really enjoy keeping X open as I read through the news, which allows me to switch back and forth between the article I’m reading and real-time reactions to it. Sometimes I’ll keep email or Slack open on the side while I’m working on something else so I don’t miss an important message or notification.

And much like the overstimulated members of Gen Z (which I am not), I sometimes like scrolling social media while engaging with some other media off to the side.

Case in point: I passively watched Netflix’s “Love is Blind” reunion while reading the gossipy tweets and Reddit posts about the main characters on the other side of the screen. This sort of TV watching behavior used to be calledsecond-screen viewing, but now it’s morphing into something new. Everything is happening on one screen, so should we call it “Duo screen viewing,” perhaps? It makes me long for even more interactive TV experiences where commentary and content are combined.

I’ve noticed another shift in my behavior since adopting the Duo as my main device. When I’m out and about, the Duo feels more like an (arguably heavier)iPhone mini. For those who still miss smaller iPhones, the Duo is the next best thing. Despite its weight, the phonefeelssmall. You can cover it with one hand; you can type with a thumb; you can reach the top and bottom easily; and you can even fit it into your front and back pockets. The Pro Max now feels unbelievably strange in my hand — how was I ever comfortable wrangling this giant rectangle?

The Duo’s small screen works well when you’re on the go, especially for short interactions like responding to a quick text or pulling up directions to a destination. It’s not as great for mindless scrolling, which I appreciate, as it forces me to engage with the real world instead of killing every moment of boredom or unease by opening up apps.

But when you’re home or somewhere with time to kill, you can unfold the screen and enjoy your apps super-sized. It’s the best of both worlds.

I find that I instinctively unfold the phone when I’m preparing to watch videos, because the larger screen is best for that. It’s also unfolded if I’m shopping, as it’s more convenient for looking at products, zooming in to examine the details, or complete checkout forms.

Generally, I also unfold the Duo when I’m actively using apps. This setup has also allowed me to rethink my Home Screen layout: With the Duo closed, I prefer to see just widgets on the small screen with key information like weather, time, battery life, and so on. Meanwhile, the only app icons on the Home Screen are those in the dock.

In the weeks since its launch, most of the apps that weren’t yet optimized for the Duo have been upgraded to support its foldable form factor. In mid-November, Apple said there wereover 200,000 Duo-ready apps, and in my experience, that certainly feels true. A majority of my so-called “daily drivers” — with the glaring exception of key Google apps like Gmail and Drive — have dropped the black band on the side of the screen that was frustrating early testers of the phone.

Most apps now take advantage of the available space, whether that’s on the Duo’s small front screen or the wider, unfolded one.

I’ve also found it interesting to see the different interpretations developers have had for how to best optimize their app for Duo.

Some have used the form factor as a way to bring in some sort of novelty: there’s a note-taking appthat opens and closes like a notebook, with pages you can write on with the Apple Pencil;a retro Walkman-like music player; atiny typewriter;a gaming handheld; a game where youclose the phone to make grilled cheese.

As much as I love the whimsy of this group of apps, I appreciate how my everyday apps feel better to use on the unfolded screen. Spotify, at last, feels less cluttered when it has more screen real estate. A number of note-taking, list-making, and calendar apps also feel somehow more usable when spread out.

The Netflix app is actually fantastic with its support for multiple viewing modes, which include playing video on the closed outer display, the “laptop” orientation with its big player controls, and the “tent” mode.

Other developers have similarly reimagined how their app would work if it had originally been designed for the Duo’s small and larger screens.

One good example of this is Sofa, a handy utility for organizing the books, movies, TV shows, podcasts, albums, and games you want to check out. When the Duo is closed, its navigation is tucked off to the right side in a vertical bar, while the main screen focuses on the items you’ve saved. But when the Duo is unfolded, the number of items displayed on the screen also expands into a two-column layout, with more of your items featured on the screen and your lists on the left side. It doesn’t feel like two different apps, but like you’ve opened up the app itself and given it more space to spread out.

articles.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.full_text:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.

"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".

He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.

"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.

The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".

Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.

A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.

A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.

Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.

She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.

Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in

Spanish election: What you need to know and what's at stake

Who to watch in Spain's election race

Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election

The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.

All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.

Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.

Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.

Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.

One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".

Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".

He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.

"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.

Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.

"So, I believe that young must mobilise."

As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".
